newsitem.title: ESTONIA: SOCCER-ESTONIA COUNTS COST OF WORLD CUP FARCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ESTONIA COUNTS COST OF WORLD CUP FARCE.

text.p: Estonia's Football Association was counting the cost on Thursday of their farcical World Cup soccer tie with Scotland while some newspapers suspected a dastardly plot to give the Scots an easy win.

The game was stopped on Wednesday after just three seconds as the Estonians failed to show up for the kick-off, brought forward to 3 p.m. (1200 GMT) from 6.45 p.m. (1545 GMT) after Scotland complained about the standard of floodlighting.

Estonian F.A. secretary-general Ainar Lettonon put the cost to Estonia at just under $250,000, including some $150,000 in lost television revenue and $100,000 from ticket refunds, the cost of security and the extra floodlighting.
"We informed them (FIFA) about the size of the material damage and then we will wait to see what they prefer to do," Lettonon told Reuters.
The saga began after Scottish coach Craig Brown said the floodlighting was the worst he had seen for an international fixture and requested FIFA, the game's ruling body, to start the match earlier.
FIFA initially backed the Estonians but after more arguing on Wednesday morning ruled in favour of the Scots.
Scotland lined up for the game at the new time but the Estonians, who said they heard of the final decision too late to get their team to the stadium, did not show up.
The referee blew the whistle to start the game but three seconds later halted it.
The match will probably be awarded to the Scots with a 3-0 win although FIFA will decide finally on November 7.
Estonian newspapers suspected a plot to give the injury-hit Scots an easy win and avoid the disgrace of defeat against such a small country as Estonia.

"The Scottish football team had to play against Estonia without six of their (best) players. To lose to Estonia, especially when there were hundreds of Scottish fans there, is something that the Scottish coach would not have dreamed of," daily newspaper Postimees said in an editorial.
"Probably we will never know whether there was such an evil plot," it added.
Estonian coach Teitur Thordarson was also bitter.
"It was not fair play, it was a nasty way to get a result," he told newspaper Sonumileht.
